articles.title: GECKO-A v1.0: exploring VOC oxidation trajectories through comparison with the master chemical mechanism
articles.titleEn: GECKO-A v1.0: exploring VOC oxidation trajectories through comparison with the master chemical mechanism
articles.abstract: Numerical models are crucial tools for understanding complex chemical systems such as the atmosphere, and their sensitivity across a range of conditions. In atmospheric chemistry models, reaction mechanisms are used to represent chemical transformations and define the underlying system of equations. Building highly explicit mechanisms that capture the full complexity of organic oxidation occurring in the atmosphere remains challenging owing to the large number of intermediates involved, the breadth of reaction pathways, and the limited availability of reliable kinetic and thermodynamic data. The Generator for Explicit Chemistry and Kinetics of Organics in the Atmosphere (GECKO-A) was developed to address these limitations by enabling the systematic construction of near-explicit mechanisms. Here, we present its first open-source release (v1.0), which incorporates updated chemical protocols and structure-activity relationships, together with its companion box model for mechanism integration. GECKO-A's performance is benchmarked through systematic comparisons with the Master Chemical Mechanism (MCM v3.3.1), based on simulations of the oxidation of five representative hydrocarbons (butane, octane, dodecane, toluene, and α -pinene) under environmental conditions ranging from urban to remote. The two approaches yield similar oxidation pathways for small and structurally simple compounds. However, differences increase with the size and complexity of the carbon backbone. In particular, the simplifications inherent to the MCM tend to limit the formation of multifunctional products and promote earlier fragmentation, resulting in notable discrepancies in the predicted volatility of secondary organic carbon and, consequently, in secondary organic aerosol yields. These discrepancies stem from how each mechanism treats multigenerational oxidation. The two approaches remain similar for early-generation products, but diverge as later generations become predominant. This divergence also extends to the water solubility of secondary organic carbon, and to its partitioning into aqueous condensed phases. GECKO-A also enables mechanism generation at different levels of chemical resolution. A reduced mechanism, denoted red-GECKO-A, is compared to the high-resolution mechanism used throughout this study. It closely reproduces the simulated oxidative trajectories for most parent compounds and scenarios. Discrepancies emerge for octane and dodecane under NO x -poor conditions.

articles.title: Hybrid implicit–explicit XFEM simulation of injection-induced seismicity: resolving multi-scale rupture nucleation and dynamics
articles.titleEn: Hybrid implicit–explicit XFEM simulation of injection-induced seismicity: resolving multi-scale rupture nucleation and dynamics
articles.abstract: This study presents a novel hybrid implicit–explicit time-integration strategy for simulating injection-induced fault reactivation within a fully coupled poroelastodynamic extended finite element (XFEM) framework. Modeling these systems is inherently challenging due to the extreme separation of temporal scales – ranging from hours to days for fluid diffusion to milliseconds for dynamic rupture. Although the fully implicit formulation can provide enhanced numerical stability, stability alone does not guarantee sufficient temporal accuracy during nonlinear fault rupture. The results demonstrate close agreement between simulations with minimum time-step sizes of 10 −5 and 10 −6 s for the investigated slip and event-scale observables on the adopted spatial mesh, indicating temporal convergence for these quantities at 10 −5 s. This time-step size is substantially smaller than the mesh-based explicit stability estimate. To reduce computational cost, the proposed strategy employs an implicit solver for quasi-static loading and nucleation and switches to a central-difference-based mechanical solver with implicit pressure integration once a prescribed slip-velocity threshold is exceeded. At a switching threshold of 0.01 m s −1 , the hybrid simulation requires approximately 10.0 h, compared with 26.4 h for the fully implicit reference, corresponding to a computational-time reduction of 62.12 %. The hybrid strategy reproduces the overall rupture sequence, stress evolution, final accumulated fault slip, and seismic moment. However, differences remain in the timing and magnitude of peak slip velocities, rupture-propagation speeds, and transient particle motion. These findings demonstrate the computational potential of the hybrid formulation for the investigated two-dimensional configuration, while highlighting the need for further assessment of transient dynamic accuracy and computational performance across different spatial discretizations and geological conditions.

articles.title: Resolving the Multiple Controls of Biomass Production Efficiency in Woody Plants
articles.titleEn: Resolving the Multiple Controls of Biomass Production Efficiency in Woody Plants
articles.abstract: Plants assimilate carbon through photosynthesis to support biomass production (BP), autotrophic respiration ( R a ) and the synthesis of non‐structural compounds. Biomass production efficiency (BPE), the fraction of assimilated carbon allocated to BP, is one key factor influencing ecosystems' potential to store carbon. However, there is no consensus on the controls of BPE, and even the sign of its response to growth temperature is unclear. By means of statistical hypothesis testing using the largest observational dataset to date on annual BPE ( n = 514 records) from evergreen and deciduous woody plants, we confirm earlier findings that BPE declines with stand age and is greater in deciduous plants. However, we also show that BPE declines toward more organic, sandy, or alkaline soils and increases with climatic aridity, while declining with warmer growing seasons and increasing with warmer winters. Such a dual temperature response is consistent with additional carbon costs due to the need for cold‐hardening processes, and reconciles contradictory published reports of both positive and negative effects of temperature on BPE. Notably, our analysis provides novel evidence that BPE is significantly higher in species associated with arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi than in those associated with ectomycorrhizal (EcM) fungi and mixed EcM–AM associations. Our analysis explains the observed BPE patterns better than dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) from the TRENDY (Trends and Drivers of the Regional‐Scale Terrestrial Sources and Sinks of Carbon Dioxide) project, which show a weaker correspondence with observations. In particular, our model captures reduced BPE in boreal regions, consistent with the predominance of ectomycorrhizal (EcM) species there. This study advances understanding of the global controls of BPE, and suggests a route toward the improved representation of plant growth in vegetation and land surface models.

articles.title: Embracing the Heterogeneity Within Particulate and Mineral‐Associated Organic Matter for the Next Generation of Soil Carbon Questions
articles.titleEn: Embracing the Heterogeneity Within Particulate and Mineral‐Associated Organic Matter for the Next Generation of Soil Carbon Questions
articles.abstract: Soil organic matter (SOM) is a complex and dynamic substrate central to the functioning of terrestrial ecosystems. Because of its heterogeneity, SOM is routinely parsed into physical fractions with more uniform composition and behavior. Over the last several years, particulate (POM) and mineral‐associated (MAOM) organic matter have become the most widely adopted of these fractions, which has given the field a shared, comparable framework for resolving the first‐order heterogeneity within SOM. As fractionation has become routine, however, it has become clear that POM and MAOM identity alone cannot resolve the finer, second‐order variation that additional mechanistic inference requires. This is in part because the fractions are operationally defined composites, whose properties vary across composition, formation pathway, and behavior. Conceptualizing them as the terminal state of analysis collapses each fraction to its central tendency, flattening the distribution and obscuring the structure on which more complex questions depend. Here we propose embracing this within‐fraction heterogeneity rather than averaging over it, treating POM and MAOM as composite distributions whose internal structure underlies the variation in how they form, persist, and function. We suggest that this view can be operationalized via two complementary approaches: tailoring fractionation methods to target subpopulations most relevant to a question, and pairing fractions with orthogonal measurements. Similar to the original framework, we do not aim to prescribe a certain methodology, but rather a way of thinking about heterogeneity within SOM, in which a separation is justified by the understanding it produces rather than the data it generates. This way of reasoning allows POM and MAOM to continue linking organic matter to its functions, and in doing so supports more informed stewardship of soil carbon.

articles.title: Enhanced weathering of glacial rock flour drives coupled inorganic and organic carbon sequestration in a five-year field experiment
articles.titleEn: Enhanced weathering of glacial rock flour drives coupled inorganic and organic carbon sequestration in a five-year field experiment
articles.abstract: Enhanced rock weathering (ERW) has been proposed as a scalable carbon dioxide removal strategy, yet long-term field-based constraints on weathering rates and associated carbon sequestration remain limited. Here, we present a 5-year field assessment of Greenlandic glacial rock flour (GRF) applied at 50 t ha −1 to a sandy agricultural soil in Denmark. Using a soil mass balance approach, based on depletion of Mg which provided the most tightly constrained weathering signal, we estimate that at least 56 % of the applied GRF dissolved over 5 years. Initial uptake of CO 2 via ERW is estimated at 3.2–4.9 t CO 2 ha −1 when accounting for carbonate speciation in the acidic soil solution, with the potential for further gains if complete downstream transport of weathering products and subsequent re-equilibration with the more alkaline marine carbonate system is assumed. In addition to inorganic carbon removal, GRF-treated plots exhibited significantly higher soil organic carbon stocks, equivalent to the storage of an additional 18.3 t CO 2 ha −1 . These results demonstrate substantial weathering and carbon sequestration over 5 years under field conditions in a temperate climate and suggest that both inorganic and organic carbon dynamics contribute meaningfully to the overall climate impact of ERW of GRF. The findings provide rare multi-year field constraints on ERW performance and underscore the importance of robust measurements for quantifying carbon removal in agricultural systems, representing the first implementation of mass balance methods within the framework of a randomized block design.

articles.title: Unreported mass movement cascades and future Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) hazard in Jammu and Kashmir, Western Himalaya
articles.titleEn: Unreported mass movement cascades and future Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) hazard in Jammu and Kashmir, Western Himalaya
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: The Warwan sub-basin in Jammu and Kashmir is a remote glaciated region containing several glacial lakes and has recently experienced population growth and infrastructure development. Due to inaccessibility and geomorphic masking, multiple mass movement events, including avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), have remained largely unreported. This study analyzes three major avalanche events from the past two decades. The September 2005 and September 2020 avalanches originated from glaciers GL-B and GL-A within the same glacier complex, while the March 2020 rock–ice avalanche initiated from the headwall of glacier GL-F in an adjacent valley and terminated before reaching its ablation zone. Runout mapping shows that the September 2020 avalanche descended from the headwall of GL-A and impacted its proglacial lake, triggering a GLOF. In contrast, the September 2005 event terminated before reaching the glacial lake that began forming in 1999 at the terminus of GL-B. Geomorphic analysis indicates persistent sediment influx from meltwater streams of GL-D and GL-E into the lake associated with GL-A, progressively infilling the lake. Continued glacier retreat caused meltwater to accumulate behind the sediment infill, dividing the lake into two disconnected lakes. Impact from the September 2020 avalanche led to complete drainage of stored water and sediment, generating a downstream debris flow. Pre- and post-GLOF imagery reveal breaching and widening of the outflow channel and deposition of a debris fan downstream. The repeated history of mass movements and continued growth of glacial lakes raise serious hazard concerns in the Warwan sub-basin. GLOF modeling identifies Lake-B as a potentially hazardous lake in its present condition, posing significant downstream risk. Settlements such as Youdu and Qaderna, along with bridges, roads, and residential structures, lie within potential GLOF inundation zones. High sediment availability from past mobilization and deposition along the valley increases the potential of debris-flow cascades, posing elevated risks to downstream infrastructure and hydropower, underscoring the need for preparedness and mitigation planning. GLOF modeling suggests that an early warning system closer to the source will be able to provide a good lead time in case of potential GLOFs in the valley.

articles.title: A Prospective Cooling Machine for the Svalbard Branch of Norwegian Atlantic Water in a Future Climate
articles.titleEn: A Prospective Cooling Machine for the Svalbard Branch of Norwegian Atlantic Water in a Future Climate
articles.abstract: The evolution of air‐sea interaction and the ocean north of Svalbard is investigated using a high‐resolution configuration of the coupled climate model HadGEM3‐GC3.1 under a high‐emission pathway (SSP5‐8.5). To the west and north of Svalbard, where the West Spitsbergen Current—the northward branch of the Norwegian Atlantic Current—carries warm and saline Atlantic Water (AW) into the Arctic, we identify a significant shift in the pattern of sea‐ice decline. In the late 20th century, the sea‐ice edge retreats gradually downstream along the current's pathway. However, in the 21st century, the ice edge retreats northward across the continental slope, leading to the simultaneous exposure of the AW core to the atmosphere. This rapid increased exposure triggers enhanced cooling and convective mixing along the AW pathway. The water column undergoes destratification due to the AW encroachment, along with mixing, resulting in a warmer and less stratified upper ocean downstream on this pathway. The potential temperature maximum of the AW shoals, increasing the potential for enhanced oceanic heat loss. A closed regional ocean heat content analysis reveals that net advective heat convergence into the region increases substantially, driving a sustained wintertime surface heat loss that stabilizes at ∼70 TW by the 2040 s. These changes suggest that a prospective “cooling machine” north of Svalbard will soon emerge in a future climate, operating at a capacity comparable to the Barents Sea and fundamentally altering the water mass transformation and heat export into the deep Arctic interior.

articles.title: Vanishing Winters and Shrinking Ice: Ecosystem Services and Societal Impacts in the Laurentian Great Lakes
articles.titleEn: Vanishing Winters and Shrinking Ice: Ecosystem Services and Societal Impacts in the Laurentian Great Lakes
articles.abstract: The Laurentian Great Lakes are undergoing rapid winter transformations, with profound implications for human societies. Winter air temperatures have increased, accelerating ice loss since the mid‐1990s. These trends are altering thermal regimes, shifting precipitation from snow to rain, and increasing winter runoff and nutrient fluxes, with cascading effects across physical, chemical, and biological systems. Using the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment framework, we synthesize how warming winters affect supporting, regulating, provisioning, and cultural ecosystem services, as well as their positive and negative socioeconomic implications for the Sustainable Development Goals. Winter warming is altering supporting services by reducing the stability and extent of under‐ice habitats that provide refugia for biodiversity and disrupting nutrient cycling. Regulating services are also affected, through increased greenhouse gas emissions, shoreline erosion and flooding, altered disease dynamics and changes in lake‐effect snowfall. Provisioning services, such as freshwater supply and fisheries, are increasingly vulnerable to harmful algal blooms, infrastructure disruptions, and reduced habitat for cold‐water species. Cultural and recreational activities including ice fishing, Indigenous traditions, and winter tourism are also threatened, while unstable ice may increase drowning risks. Although reduced ice cover may benefit navigation and summer recreation, these gains are outweighed by broader ecological and cultural losses. Collectively, these findings show that lake ice functions as a mediating variable regulating interconnected ecological and societal processes. Its loss threatens ecosystem resilience and heightens socioeconomic vulnerabilities for the 40 million people who depend on the Great Lakes. Addressing these challenges will require cross‐border cooperation.

articles.title: Prediction of Escaped Powerline‐Caused Fires in Alberta, Canada
articles.titleEn: Prediction of Escaped Powerline‐Caused Fires in Alberta, Canada
articles.abstract: Powerlines have increasingly become a source of wildfire ignitions, contributing to more escaped and catastrophic fires during extreme fire weather. Temporary power shutoffs are implemented to reduce this risk, yet decisions on their implementations are often based on limited scientific evidence. Focusing on the boreal forests in Alberta, Canada, we developed an integrated framework to assess the likelihood of Escaped powerline‐caused fires (EPF) (EPFs) from occurrence and early spread perspectives. Using records of powerline‐caused fires from 1990 to 2023, we integrated MaxEnt and machine‐learning models to predict occurrence and escape probability from fire weather, fuels, and topography at the regional scale, overcoming the reliance on detailed powerline operational parameters. articles.title: Integration of Aerosol–Cloud Interactions With a Land‐Atmosphere Coupled Model in the Gray Zone
articles.titleEn: Integration of Aerosol–Cloud Interactions With a Land‐Atmosphere Coupled Model in the Gray Zone
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Clouds strongly impact net surface radiation, creating differential heating patterns, and trigger land breezes that in turn organize cloud development. These dial processes determine the location of persistent ecohydrological regimes at local scales. Aerosol–cloud interactions (ACI) directly impact the diurnal cycle of cloud optical depth, and therefore the surface energy budget; yet they are generally not explicitly represented in studies of land‐atmosphere interactions. To address this gap, a 3D Large‐Eddy Simulation model was modified to describe ACI in the gray zone. The goal is to simulate realistic cumulus cloud dynamics consistent with the spatial dynamics of land surface moisture and temperature, and associated boundary layer processes. The model is tested and evaluated using simulations at hectometer resolution with prescribed diurnal surface heating corresponding to idealized wet (low Bowen ratio [LBR]) and dry (high Bowen ratio [HBR]) surface boundary conditions. Expected cloud sensitivity is well captured: compared to LBR, HBR clouds have a significantly higher cloud base (about 1 km), up to 50% reduction in total cloud fraction, and cloudiness ends earlier by about 2 hr due to enhanced turbulence and lower moisture availability. Analyses of the evolution of 3D cloud drop size distributions show that the model captures the cloud life cycle, including aerosol activation, condensational growth, enhanced collision‐coalescence, and aerosol regeneration. The results show that resolved eddy‐scale (sub‐km) within‐cloud circulations modulate cloud microphysical structure by locally altering supersaturation at minute timescales. Successive aerosol regeneration yields coarser cloud condensation nuclei, producing a coarse‐aerosol mode, and impacting mid‐day cloud fraction and cloudiness persistence.

articles.title: Advancing Satellite Solar‐Induced Chlorophyll Fluorescence Data Assimilation in Land Surface Models: An Assessment Over Boreal Evergreen Needleleaf Forests
articles.titleEn: Advancing Satellite Solar‐Induced Chlorophyll Fluorescence Data Assimilation in Land Surface Models: An Assessment Over Boreal Evergreen Needleleaf Forests
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Boreal forests represent about 20% of the global forest carbon sink and contribute to climate change mitigation, yet land surface models (LSMs) struggle to simulate their gross primary production (GPP). Space‐borne observations of solar‐induced fluorescence (SIF) have been used to improve LSM GPP through data assimilation. However, previous work has shown that assimilating SIF alone can degrade GPP for some vegetation types, highlighting the need for enhanced process representation and tightly constrained parameters. Uncertainties in the representation of non‐photochemical quenching (NPQ), which regulates the SIF‐GPP relationship, further complicate this challenge. Here, we develop a data assimilation strategy to assess the complementarity of satellite SIF from TROPOMI and in situ GPP in constraining GPP dynamics simulated by the ORCHIDEE LSM over boreal evergreen needleleaf forests. We evaluate this framework using two NPQ schemes, a process‐based formulation separating sustained and reversible components, and a generic model representing total NPQ. After assimilation, evaluation against independent SIF grid cells and flux sites shows improved seasonal cycles of both SIF and GPP. Regional‐scale simulations better match independent GPP products (FLUXSAT and FLUXCOM‐X‐BASE) over 2001–2020, with over 77% RMSD reduction in the mean seasonal cycle versus the prior, largely reflecting the recalibration of model parameters after implementation of the new radiative transfer scheme. SIF‐GPP co‐assimilation outperforms GPP‐only assimilation for the GPP latitudinal profile, and also for the GPP mean seasonal cycle in three out of four cases. Although the two NPQ models affect the simulated SIF seasonal cycle differently, their performances after assimilation are similar.

articles.title: Zero emissions commitment depends on warming level
articles.titleEn: Zero emissions commitment depends on warming level
articles.abstract: When anthropogenic CO 2 emissions cease, global temperature does not stabilize immediately. The resulting global temperature change, the zero emissions commitment, is central to carbon budget assessments and understanding reversibility of global warming, yet its dependence on prior warming levels remains unclear. Here we show, using zero-emission simulations with the UK Earth System Model (UKESM1.2) across global warming levels of 1.5–5 K, that the zero emissions commitment stays near zero up to 2 K but becomes positive at higher warming levels, reaching 0.4–0.6 K after ~ 150 years. This dependence indicates that stabilizing or reversing warming becomes progressively more difficult as peak temperature rises. We identify the mechanism behind this behaviour: stronger warming from higher radiative disequilibrium and weakening carbon sinks, driven by saturated land carbon uptake and the reduced radiative impact of CO 2 drawdown at higher background CO 2 concentrations. Higher peak warming therefore commits the planet to additional warming, limiting temperature-overshoot reversibility.

articles.title: Assessing the Effects of Climate Change Projections on Water Fluxes and Streamwater NO 3 –N in Lowland Catchments Using Isotope‐Aided Water Quality Modeling
articles.titleEn: Assessing the Effects of Climate Change Projections on Water Fluxes and Streamwater NO 3 –N in Lowland Catchments Using Isotope‐Aided Water Quality Modeling
articles.abstract: Understanding how climate change alters hydrological connectivity and associated nitrate dynamics remains a key challenge in lowland, mixed land‐use catchments. Here, we use a tracer‐aided, fully distributed ecohydrological modeling framework to investigate how future climate conditions may influence water fluxes and nitrate dynamics in such systems, using the Demnitzer Mill Creek catchment in Germany as an exemplar. To provide mechanistic insight into hydrological transport and biogeochemical processing, we applied diagnostic metrics based on water age and the Damköhler (Da) number, which links water residence times with reaction timescales. Results indicate that projected warming and a shift of precipitation toward winter progressively strengthen hydrological connectivity, leading to increased infiltration, evapotranspiration, and subsurface flow contributions. This stronger connectivity reorganizes nitrate transport across the catchment, with enhanced lateral redistribution, declining agricultural soil nitrate stocks, and lower stream nitrate concentrations. At the same time, processing times decrease more strongly than hydrological exposure times, increasing Da number and indicating a shift toward stronger reaction dominance. Uncertainty arises from climate forcing projections, simplified representations of subsurface processes, and assumptions regarding future agricultural practices. Overall, the results highlight the coupled role of transport and processing of nutrients and the value of coupled tracer‐aided water quality models. The findings also emphasize hydrological connectivity as a key control on future water quality.

articles.title: Quantifying Ion‐Specific Effects on the Size‐Exclusion Transport of Multi‐Sized Colloids in Porous Media Using a Novel Synthetic DNA Labeling Approach
articles.titleEn: Quantifying Ion‐Specific Effects on the Size‐Exclusion Transport of Multi‐Sized Colloids in Porous Media Using a Novel Synthetic DNA Labeling Approach
articles.abstract: Colloids strongly adsorb pollutants and promote their co‐transport in aquatic environments, posing substantial ecological contamination risks. However, quantifying the size exclusion effect (SEE), a critical mechanism that enhances colloid transport, remains challenging in multi‐sized colloid systems, owing to limited high‐resolution labeling methods and ion‐induced dynamic aggregation. Here, we developed a high‐resolution DNA‐based tracing framework that employs synthetic DNA fragments to individually label multi‐sized colloids (0.1, 0.2, 0.5, and 1.0 μm), and utilizes quantitative real‐time PCR (qPCR) to quantify their transport behavior in saturated quartz sand under the typical environmental ions (NaCl/CaCl 2 ). The results demonstrated that Ca 2+ promoted colloid aggregation and retention more strongly than Na + , thereby modifying size‐exclusion behavior, although the magnitude of SEE depended on colloid size and transport conditions. While the SEE generally exhibited a positive size dependence in the single‐sized system, the multi‐sized system exhibited higher SEE for 0.1 and 0.2 μm colloids relative to their single‐sized counterparts under certain solution chemistry conditions. This discrepancy may be attributed to pore blockage caused by larger colloids within the multi‐sized system. Furthermore, two transport patterns, blocking and ripening, were identified from the breakthrough curves of DNA‐labeled colloids. Correlation analysis revealed that the SEE parameter ( γ ) was positively correlated with the normalized retention parameter ( S max / C 0 ) under blocking conditions ( r = 0.655). This study highlights the effectiveness of synthetic DNA labeling approach in tracking the transport of multi‐sized colloids, providing new insights into the fate of colloids in natural and engineered porous systems.
articles.abstractEn: Colloids strongly adsorb pollutants and promote their co‐transport in aquatic environments, posing substantial ecological contamination risks. Here, we developed a high‐resolution DNA‐based tracing framework that employs synthetic DNA fragments to individually label multi‐sized colloids (0.1, 0.2, 0.5, and 1.0 μm), and utilizes quantitative real‐time PCR (qPCR) to quantify their transport behavior in saturated quartz sand under the typical environmental ions (NaCl/CaCl 2 ). The results demonstrated that Ca 2+ promoted colloid aggregation and retention more strongly than Na + , thereby modifying size‐exclusion behavior, although the magnitude of SEE depended on colloid size and transport conditions. While the SEE generally exhibited a positive size dependence in the single‐sized system, the multi‐sized system exhibited higher SEE for 0.1 and 0.2 μm colloids relative to their single‐sized counterparts under certain solution chemistry conditions. This discrepancy may be attributed to pore blockage caused by larger colloids within the multi‐sized system. Furthermore, two transport patterns, blocking and ripening, were identified from the breakthrough curves of DNA‐labeled colloids. Correlation analysis revealed that the SEE parameter ( γ ) was positively correlated with the normalized retention parameter ( S max / C 0 ) under blocking conditions ( r = 0.655). This study highlights the effectiveness of synthetic DNA labeling approach in tracking the transport of multi‐sized colloids, providing new insights into the fate of colloids in natural and engineered porous systems.

articles.title: Merging Regional Climate Models and Remote Sensing Observations to Better Estimate Mountain Snow Water Equivalent
articles.titleEn: Merging Regional Climate Models and Remote Sensing Observations to Better Estimate Mountain Snow Water Equivalent
articles.abstract: Large‐scale, high‐resolution estimation of snow water equivalent (SWE) in mountainous regions remains challenging. Continental‐scale approaches, including SWE reconstruction and regional climate model (RCM) simulations, are computationally expensive at high resolutions. We present Blender, a variational data assimilation method that improves modeled SWE and snowfall time series by modifying snowpack mass and energy balance while minimizing changes to input precipitation and energy fluxes, subject to remotely sensed snow cover fraction constraints. Blender combines the advantages of RCM simulation and SWE reconstruction and can be applied as a post‐processing step to many gridded snow data sets. We tested Blender at 500 m resolution in the Tuolumne watershed, Sierra Nevada, USA, during water years 2013, 2016, and 2017 (low, average, and high snow accumulation). We tested Blender with prior inputs from an RCM and ERA5‐Land (ERA5L), and evaluated posterior (output) performance using 18 Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) flights, and compared its performance with the Western United States Snow Reanalysis (WUS‐SR). Blender improved spatial SWE patterns relative to ASO in all years for the RCM prior (RMSEP: 17.2% → 11.5%, R : 0.39 → 0.72) and ERA5L prior (RMSEP: 13.9% → 12.9%, R : 0.003 → 0.59), approaching WUS‐SR performance (RMSEP = 9.5%, R = 0.82). Blender improved snow water storage (SWS) estimates for the RCM prior but not for ERA5L prior, although ERA5L posterior SWS remained reasonably accurate (median absolute error of 27%). Blender provides a flexible and efficient pathway toward higher‐resolution, large‐scale SWE estimation in mountainous regions.

articles.title: Leveraging leaf-level optimality processes with explicit acclimation improves global GPP representation in an individual-based DGVM (LPJ-GUESS v4.1.1)
articles.titleEn: Leveraging leaf-level optimality processes with explicit acclimation improves global GPP representation in an individual-based DGVM (LPJ-GUESS v4.1.1)
articles.abstract: Vegetation models are indispensable tools for investigating and projecting the terrestrial carbon cycle, both as standalone models and embedded in global climate models. However, current models vary widely in their representation of ecosystem processes and consequently in their projected future carbon dynamics. Eco-evolutionary optimality (EEO) approaches, which derive and test hypotheses about optimal plant behaviour under specific environmental conditions as a consequence of natural selection, have been proposed as a means to improve the reliability of vegetation models and the robustness of their future projections. Here we embed EEO-derived models for photosynthesis and leaf dark respiration, and their acclimation to changing conditions, into the widely used LPJ-GUESS vegetation model. We evaluated the simulated gross primary production (GPP) patterns against remotely-sensed GPP derived from sun-induced fluorescence and found that the EEO configurations improved the spatial distributions (a mean reduction in error of 15 % across gridcells) and global interannual variability (a mean reduction in error of 32 % after accounting for differences in global totals) compared to the standard version of LPJ-GUESS. Evaluation against GPP fluxes from eddy flux covariance measurements also showed improved performance, the R 2 of 5 d GPP increased from 0.45 to 0.48 (averaged across 147 sites). The simulated global carbon pools, fluxes, burnt area and biome distributions were not impacted substantially. The improvements were achieved with no alteration to processes except photosynthesis, respiration and plant water uptake, and with no recalibration or tuning. The EEO configuration also reduced model run time and eliminated the need for poorly-constrained PFT-dependent parameters governing the temperature response of photosynthesis. As well as being a tangible improvement to LPJ-GUESS, this study further confirms the usefulness of EEO approaches to improve global vegetation models.

articles.title: Global-scale meteorological-to-groundwater drought propagation and the drivers and patterns of multi-year groundwater drought
articles.titleEn: Global-scale meteorological-to-groundwater drought propagation and the drivers and patterns of multi-year groundwater drought
articles.abstract: Groundwater stores a third of all global freshwater and supports water supply, irrigation and ecosystems across the world. As such, groundwater drought can have wide-reaching financial, social and environmental impacts, particularly when drought events are prolonged or multi-year. Although recent work has made significant progress in understanding the drivers and patterns of multi-year meteorological droughts, we do not know how this signal translates into multi-year groundwater drought, where subsurface processes, anthropogenic influences and abstractions can alter the meteorological signal. This is particularly true at the global-scale, where a major barrier to understanding large-scale groundwater drought dynamics is the difficulty of obtaining consistent and comprehensive groundwater data. In this research, we use a new global hyper-resolution (∼1 km) groundwater dataset to investigate the global patterns and drivers of groundwater drought from 1960–2019, with a specific focus on multi-year events. We start by characterizing the propagation of meteorological (represented by SPEI-12) to groundwater drought, evaluating how and to what extent the sub-surface plays a role in modulating the meteorological drought signal. Subsequently, we define three global groundwater response types that provide a framework for understanding the processes and geo-physical drivers of normal versus multi-year groundwater droughts. We find that 35 % of global groundwater grid cells have an average groundwater drought duration which is multi-year. In 83 % of these locations, the subsurface extends the meteorological drought signal, whereas in the remaining 17 %, groundwater drought duration appears to be primarily driven by meteorological anomalies. Our analysis offers new insights into global-scale drought exposure by identifying regions which have been most vulnerable to multi-year groundwater drought in the past, as well as those which might be more vulnerable in the future. Importantly, our typology also highlights areas where multi-year groundwater droughts can be anticipated based on meteorological drought anomalies and can therefore inform strategies for managing and mitigating future water scarcity risks.

articles.title: Monthly-updated territorial fossil CO 2 emissions estimates for Japan
articles.titleEn: Monthly-updated territorial fossil CO 2 emissions estimates for Japan
articles.abstract: We present a low-lag, monthly dataset of emissions of carbon dioxide from fossil fuel consumption and industrial processes in Japan, derived directly from official activity data and starting in 2007. Such estimates will be crucial for near-real-time monitoring of emissions and making swift policy responses accordingly. When aggregated, our estimates replicate the annual data published through the UNFCCC national inventory report very well, with only small discrepancies which we describe and quantify. The dataset is produced with a lag of 2 months and can be used to estimate the annual emissions a year ahead of the official estimates submitted to the UNFCCC, and also provides a better starting point for short-term emissions projections. Data are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20023226 (Kunimitsu and Andrew, 2026).

articles.title: The Standardized Soil Moisture-Temperature Compound Index (SSTCI): daily scale global data set and event catalogue for compound dry-hot extremes (1961–2023)
articles.titleEn: The Standardized Soil Moisture-Temperature Compound Index (SSTCI): daily scale global data set and event catalogue for compound dry-hot extremes (1961–2023)
articles.abstract: Compound dry-hot extremes (CDHEs) are among the most damaging climate hazards. Most metrics used to diagnose them are estimated at monthly or seasonal resolution or rely on precipitation-based drought proxies that can miss fast soil moisture-driven land–atmosphere feedbacks. This paper delivers two tightly linked products for global CDHE monitoring over land (excluding Antarctica) at 0.1° resolution for 1961–2023: (i) a continuous, daily severity index, i.e. the Standardized Soil Moisture–Temperature Compound Index (SSTCI), and (ii) a companion, event-based CDHE catalogue derived from SSTCI. SSTCI is constructed by first quantifying grid specific soil moisture memory using dry-down events, fitting an exponential decay to estimate a characteristic dry-down timescale ( τ ). This memory is used to compute a Standardized Antecedent Soil Moisture Index (SASMI), which is paired with a daily Standardized Temperature Index (STI). SASMI and STI are then integrated using a Frank copula to represent their joint probability, which is transformed to a standardized normal variate to yield SSTCI, providing a spatially comparable daily measure of compound dry-hot stress. To move from daily index values to physically interpretable hazards, we post-process the daily SSTCI series by discarding very short extreme spells and merging those separated by only brief interruptions, so that fragmented detections become single coherent events; the resulting catalogue carries event timing and magnitude descriptors suitable for event-based statistics. Our evaluation shows broad agreement between SASMI (SSTCI) and established drought (compound) metrics and vegetation stress. Moreover, SSTCI captures the timing and evolution of well documented CDHEs across multiple regions and timescales when applied to case studies. Together, the resulting SSTCI fields and event catalogue provide a consistent, daily scale foundation for global monitoring, process attribution of land–atmosphere feedback, and early-warning applications for compound dry-hot hazards. Data introduced in this paper are openly accessible from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18280747 (SSTCI) (Aftab et al., 2026c) and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20826759 (CDHE event catalogue) (Aftab et al., 2026b).

articles.title: Divergent Patterns of Interactions Between Dissolved Organic Matter and Microbial Communities in Mangroves and Salt Marshes
articles.titleEn: Divergent Patterns of Interactions Between Dissolved Organic Matter and Microbial Communities in Mangroves and Salt Marshes
articles.abstract: Mangroves and salt marshes are major blue carbon reservoirs, where dissolved organic matter (DOM) dynamics are co‐regulated by primary production, microbial transformation, and environmental conditions. Understanding whether these two coastal wetlands exhibit fundamentally different DOM–microbe interaction patterns is critical for assessing blue carbon functioning. However, such interactions and their environmental determinants remain unclear. Here, we conduct a continental‐scale comparison between mangroves and salt marshes spanning ~5000 km of China's coastline to elucidate the linkages between DOM molecules and microbial communities. DOM and bacterial β‐diversity are positively correlated in both wetlands, but their respective distance–decay relationships are significant only in salt marshes. DOM–microbe co‐occurrence networks are bacteria‐dominated in both wetlands, but are more complex and positively linked in mangroves, whereas negatively linked in salt marshes. DOM‐gene networks show that carbon fixation and methanogenesis genes are primarily associated with recalcitrant DOM in mangroves, but with labile DOM in salt marshes. Soil pH, together with mean annual temperature, dissolved organic carbon, soil organic carbon, total nitrogen, and amorphous calcium, collectively influence the divergences in DOM composition, microbial community structure, and carbon metabolic functions. These findings offer key insights into DOM–microbe interaction mechanisms and their divergent patterns across “blue carbon” ecosystems.

articles.title: Phenology and surface energy balance changes across northern lands
articles.titleEn: Phenology and surface energy balance changes across northern lands
articles.abstract: Plant phenological shifts – notably earlier start (SOS) and later end (EOS) of the growing season – affect surface albedo, latent and sensible heat fluxes, and ultimately the surface temperature. The magnitude and spatial variability of these effects remain uncertain. Using Earth observation and reanalysis data (2001–2021), we quantify the sensitivity of surface energy fluxes to SOS and EOS changes across northern lands (> 30° N), and we report uncertainties and convergence across multiple independent datasets. Spatially-aggregated results show that an earlier SOS is generally associated with decreased albedo by up to 0.003 d −1 (needleleaf forests and tundra), and increased latent heat fluxes by 0.47 Wm-2d-1 (spatial median), ranging from 0.15 Wm-2d-1 (croplands) to 0.68 Wm-2d-1 (mixed forests). Delays in EOS are also associated with decreases in albedo, though much smaller in magnitude, and with increases in latent heat flux – up to ∼0.14 Wm-2d-1 in mixed forests – with weaker and more variable responses across other land-cover types. Datasets reveal large spatial variability and discrepancies in the responses of the sensible heat fluxes and thus evaporative fraction. Across datasets, earlier SOS is consistently associated with increased latent heat flux, and the concurrent evidence from evaporative fraction suggests a shift towards enhanced latent cooling. These findings are consistent with a phenology-driven negative feedback on surface warming through enhanced evaporative cooling, although causal attribution from observational analyses alone is not possible.

articles.title: Field surveying and numerical simulation of the Typhoon Hato storm surge event in Guangdong province, China
articles.titleEn: Field surveying and numerical simulation of the Typhoon Hato storm surge event in Guangdong province, China
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: In 2017, Typhoon Hato hitting Zhuhai city, Guangdong province, caused a severe storm surge disaster. In this study, a systematic field survey of the “Hato” storm surge was conducted and the numerical modeling of inundation extent and depth was performed. The survey integrated floating debris tracking, inundation tracing, and local inquiries to determine the seawater inundation edge points, water depths, and overall extent of the flooding. Combined with field reconnaissance, the mechanisms damaging typical hazard-bearing bodies during marine disasters were clarified, and the effects of the “Hato” storm surge were analyzed. Inundated areas were distributed in coastal cities, with the maximum inundation depth up to about 2 m, and the inundated area exceeding 54.08 km 2 . Compared to historical storm surge records, Typhoon Hato ranked as the fourth most severe and stands as one of the most devastating storm surges to impact Guangdong province over the past decade. In addition, the proposed model can reproduce this typhoon and storm surge event, which was evaluated by comparing field observations with numerical simulations, showing good consistency with the observed flooding records. These results could provide detailed data and decision support, which can be used as guidance for the mitigation of future storm surges in coastal areas.

articles.title: Persistence of scour at bridges using stochastic simulations
articles.titleEn: Persistence of scour at bridges using stochastic simulations
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: The stochastic and deterministic properties of the scouring process at bridges are analysed by coupling synthetic streamflow generations with a scour and fill model considering the upstream sediment supply. Streamflow was generated using the asymmetric moving-average (AMA) scheme that preserves the Hurst-Kolmogorov (HK) dynamics, the second-order dependence structure, time asymmetry, and the first four statistical moments of the marginal distribution. Stationarity, homogeneity, and ergodicity of the streamflow and scouring processes were assumed. Monte Carlo analyses covered 12 000 realisations for each of the three considered scenarios with different upstream sediment supply. Extreme scour events were assessed using annual maxima with GEV fitting and compared against the equilibrium scour. The dependence structure was identified with the climacogram and climacospectrum stochastic tools and fitted with a filtered HK model (FHK-CD). The obtained results show a multi-scale dynamics of the scouring process with rough and weak persistent behaviour ( M ≈0.40; H ≈0.60), while envelopes span from antipersistent to strongly persistent scour regimes ( H up to ≈0.86) depending on the upstream sediment supply. It is worth noting that the upstream sediment supply reduced the envelope variability and modified the extreme scour values. Additionally, synchronisation between extreme events of streamflow and scour showed a weak correspondence (Critical Success Index ≈0.15–0.60), indicating that streamflow extremes do not systematically translate into scour extremes. Finally, scour depths with a given return period (computed from scour time series) increase with upstream sediment supply.

articles.title: Multi-scale dynamics and mesoscale drivers of the catastrophic September 2022 Marche (central Italy) flood
articles.titleEn: Multi-scale dynamics and mesoscale drivers of the catastrophic September 2022 Marche (central Italy) flood
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: The catastrophic flood that hit the Marche region (central Italy) on 15 September 2022 has been analyzed using high-resolution Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations. The convective rainfall event responsible for the flood was favored by the passage of warm, moist air masses that interacted with the central Apennines. The convective cells, triggered by the rough orography of the area, formed quasi-stationary bands that caused high rainfall accumulation in limited areas. The formation of these rainbands was sustained by the interaction between the low-level flow and the local topography, which generated a persistent low-level convergence line extending downwind from Mount Amiata northeastward towards the Apennines. The observed vertical profile upstream of the orography reveals that the instability was initially suppressed by an inversion layer and was released only when the humid air arrived at low levels and eroded the inhibition. Furthermore, the simulations suggest that gravity waves induced by the mountains may have helped to sustain the vertical motion of the impinging air, and highlight the role of upper-level dynamics (passage of a jet streak). The comparison with surface stations shows that the simulation underestimates peak accumulations (160–180 mm simulated vs. over 400 mm observed), delays the event by 1–2 h, and misses the final phase. However, overall the model captures the system's spatial position, orientation, and quasi-stationary evolution associated with orographic anchoring. Rather than evaluating predictive skill in an operational-like perspective, this study investigates the physical precursors and dynamical mechanisms of the event. Sensitivity experiments reveal a strong dependence on initial and boundary conditions. A comparison of the control run (forced with Global Data Assimilation System (GDAS) analysis/forecasts) with a simulation driven by European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) analysis/forecasts shows a strong sensitivity to the low-level dynamics. Although the large-scale upper-level forcing is almost identical, the ECMWF-driven forecast fails to reproduce the correct amount and distribution of rainfall due to a weaker surface pressure gradient, reduced moisture advection, and lower instability at the time of the event. Specifically, the simulation forced with the ECMWF data anticipates the arrival of the moist air mass, determining a timing mismatch between the low-level supply of moist air (and the consequent release of instability) and the upper-level forcing. This lack of synchronization shifts the rainfall away from the observed area.

The observed vertical profile upstream of the orography reveals that the instability was initially suppressed by an inversion layer and was released only when the humid air arrived at low levels and eroded the inhibition. Furthermore, the simulations suggest that gravity waves induced by the mountains may have helped to sustain the vertical motion of the impinging air, and highlight the role of upper-level dynamics (passage of a jet streak). The comparison with surface stations shows that the simulation underestimates peak accumulations (160–180 mm simulated vs. over 400 mm observed), delays the event by 1–2 h, and misses the final phase. However, overall the model captures the system's spatial position, orientation, and quasi-stationary evolution associated with orographic anchoring. Rather than evaluating predictive skill in an operational-like perspective, this study investigates the physical precursors and dynamical mechanisms of the event. Sensitivity experiments reveal a strong dependence on initial and boundary conditions. A comparison of the control run (forced with Global Data Assimilation System (GDAS) analysis/forecasts) with a simulation driven by European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) analysis/forecasts shows a strong sensitivity to the low-level dynamics. Although the large-scale upper-level forcing is almost identical, the ECMWF-driven forecast fails to reproduce the correct amount and distribution of rainfall due to a weaker surface pressure gradient, reduced moisture advection, and lower instability at the time of the event. Specifically, the simulation forced with the ECMWF data anticipates the arrival of the moist air mass, determining a timing mismatch between the low-level supply of moist air (and the consequent release of instability) and the upper-level forcing. This lack of synchronization shifts the rainfall away from the observed area.

articles.title: Technical note: Evaluation of snow water equivalent from large-scale land-surface products over Italy
articles.titleEn: Technical note: Evaluation of snow water equivalent from large-scale land-surface products over Italy
articles.abstract: Snow water equivalent (SWE) is a critical hydrological variable for water resource management in mountainous regions, where seasonal snowpacks function as natural reservoirs regulating streamflow and water supply. While high-resolution, observation-constrained regional or national snow products provide reliable daily SWE estimates at fine spatial resolution (less than 1 km), their limited temporal coverage often restricts their use for long-term hydro-climatological studies. Large-scale land-surface products, in which SWE is derived from land-surface model simulations driven by atmospheric reanalyses or regional dynamical downscaling systems, provide multi-decadal coverage, but their reliability may be affected by biases in meteorological forcing, limited topographic representation, and simplified snow process parameterisation, requiring rigorous regional evaluation. This study evaluates the SWE estimates of three large-scale land-surface products, i.e., the global ERA5-Land, the European CERRA-Land, and the Italian VHR-REA_IT, against the national reference dataset IT-SNOW across Italy. The analysis combines grid-scale bias assessment of mean annual SWE and snow cover duration with temporal correlation analysis of daily SWE series, and is complemented by an evaluation of precipitation and temperature biases in each product, providing insight into how each product represents the atmospheric conditions governing snow accumulation and ablation and thereby supporting the interpretation of the identified SWE discrepancies. The results show clear regional differences in product performance, with no single product performing best across all metrics. ERA5-Land shows the strongest temporal correlation with IT-SNOW, but tends to overestimate mean annual SWE and snow cover duration in the Alps. CERRA-Land shows more moderate biases than ERA5-Land in the Italian Alps, but generally underestimates mean annual SWE across most subregions, where autumn and winter precipitation deficits in the forcing limit snow accumulation. Across the Apennines, both ERA5-Land and CERRA-Land tend to underestimate SWE and snow cover duration, particularly in the northern sectors. VHR-REA_IT shows widespread underestimation and the weakest temporal correspondence with IT-SNOW despite its finer grid spacing, which may be due to its fully coupled atmosphere–land architecture with no assimilation of meteorological observations. Overall, the results suggest that forcing biases explain a substantial part of the observed SWE discrepancies, although not all of them. This study provides useful insights for the use of SWE estimates from large-scale land-surface products in long-term hydro-climatological assessments over Italy and helps to understand whether the products can be used to evaluate snow dynamics in mountainous regions lacking high-quality benchmark estimates.

articles.title: Technical note: Benefits of Bayesian estimation of model parameters in a large hydrological model ensemble
articles.titleEn: Technical note: Benefits of Bayesian estimation of model parameters in a large hydrological model ensemble
articles.abstract: Quantifying and mitigating parametric and structural uncertainties in hydrological models are crucial to accurately understand and predict the rainfall-runoff process. Despite recent advances in Bayesian approaches for quantifying structural uncertainty using very large hydrological model ensembles, the simultaneous quantification of both parametric and structural uncertainties has yet to be implemented since previous works on large model ensembles have relied on deterministic optimization of parameters. Here we present the potential benefits of Bayesian estimation of parametric uncertainty within a large hydrological model ensemble. We find that Bayesian estimation of model parameters (more generally, change in calibration methods) potentially influences the interpretation of model comparisons. Specifically, Bayesian parametric uncertainty quantification greatly benefits complex models with many parameters, thereby affecting discussions of the appropriate level of model complexity. We also find that Bayesian parametric uncertainty quantification does not substantially improve multi-model hydrological predictions. The adverse effects of parameter misspecification in individual models are effectively mitigated by combining models with diverse structures. Thus, the high computational cost of Bayesian parameter estimation is not paid for to improve rainfall-runoff analysis in a large hydrological model ensemble.

articles.title: HESS Opinions: Operationalizing sociohydrology from systems thinking to systems doing for sustainable and resilient water management
articles.titleEn: HESS Opinions: Operationalizing sociohydrology from systems thinking to systems doing for sustainable and resilient water management
articles.abstract: Sociohydrology has advanced explanations of coupled human-water systems, but its translation into decision support remains uneven. We propose two complementary approaches to move from systems thinking to systems doing: (i) canonical feedback structures, which describe the main components of human-water systems and how they interact and enable comparison across cases while accounting for important local differences; and (ii) critical pathways, which trace how management actions propagate through these components to produce outcomes, including unintended consequences. Drawing on cases such as the levee effect and reservoir effect, these approaches connect system understanding with intervention design, monitoring, and adaptive learning. We then propose a minimal “systems-doing loop” that links the decision setting, feedback mapping, pathway tracing, indicator selection, and iteration, with equity and legitimacy treated as explicit constraints on useful knowledge and acceptable action. This framing complements predictive modelling and integrated water resources management by accounting for potential unintended consequences in decision-making and clarifying what to monitor and revisit as systems change.

articles.title: Role of hydrometeorological variables and catchment area to flood generation over the monsoonal climate region of India
articles.titleEn: Role of hydrometeorological variables and catchment area to flood generation over the monsoonal climate region of India
articles.abstract: Indian River basins experience frequent flooding during the Indian summer monsoon and pose several challenges for the region's large population, yet the hydrometeorological and catchment-scale drivers that control flood processes remain poorly explored across India. To effectively manage flood risk in the densely populated Indian region, it is essential to understand how the temporal properties of precipitation and runoff generate floods across different aridity regimes within a large catchment, and which specific areas of a large, climatically heterogeneous basin generate the runoff that drives downstream flood peaks. In this study, we address these gaps and examine the role of hydrometeorological variables (such as precipitation and surface runoff) and catchment area in the flood occurrence in the Godavari River basin (one of the largest river basins in the Indian Subcontinent) using observed and VIC-simulated datasets. Based on the temporal analysis of precipitation, runoff, and streamflow, we show that the majority of floods in the semi-humid sub-basins (Tekra, Pathagudam, Perur, and Polavaram) are predominantly associated with 10 to 11 d of accumulated precipitation, having multiple high-intensity precipitation events prior to flood. In contrast, the floods in the semi-arid region of Godavari (Mancherial sub-basin) are triggered by a single high-intensity precipitation day and are associated with short-duration (2 d) accumulated precipitation. In addition to temporal analysis, we performed Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) analysis using precipitation, runoff, and streamflow data to identify the specific sub-regions that disproportionately generate flood-causing runoff (flood-dominant catchment areas). Our results demonstrate that central and downstream areas of the basin contribute dominantly to flood occurrence, generating substantially higher runoff in the Tekra sub-basin. Overall, this study moves beyond basin-averaged flood attribution and advances understanding of flood-generating mechanisms over the Godavari River basin, which can be helpful for duration-informed forecasting and catchment-scale flood management during the monsoonal climate of the Indian Subcontinent.

articles.title: MLAWind: a monthly sea surface wind dataset derived from an interpretable machine learning approach integrating in-situ observations and satellite data
articles.titleEn: MLAWind: a monthly sea surface wind dataset derived from an interpretable machine learning approach integrating in-situ observations and satellite data
articles.abstract: A gridded sea surface wind dataset with long temporal coverage is crucial for understanding atmospheric circulation changes and air–sea interactions at different time scales. This study employs an interpretable machine learning model based on random forest algorithm to generate a 1° × 1° monthly sea surface wind dataset (MLAWind) from 1950 to 2023, covering the near-global ocean within 60° S–60° N. The data reconstruction model integrates the Cross-Calibrated Multi-Platform (CCMP) satellite data and the spatially sparse long-term International Comprehensive Ocean-Atmosphere Data Set (ICOADS), exhibiting robust interpretability and generalization capability. Quantitative validations against satellite and in-situ data indicate that MLAWind achieves better consistency with observations than most reanalysis datasets, maintaining robust performance during both training (1993–2022) and testing periods (2023). The performance of MLAWind since 1950 is assessed across multiple time scales. Its characteristics in climatology, annual cycle, and inter-annual variability are comparable to those of reanalysis datasets, even during the non-satellite period prior to 1993. Independent coral records from 1950–1982 are employed as proxy indicators to evaluate long-term sea surface wind trends. The trend derived from MLAWind is corroborated by these proxies, exhibiting significantly higher temporal correlation than those obtained from reanalysis products. MLAWind demonstrates a more reliable reconstruction of long-term sea surface wind variability during historical periods since 1950. The results indicate that MLAWind serves as a robust data resource for global climate change research. The reconstructed MLAWind dataset is publicly accessible at https://doi.org/10.12157/IOCAS.20250707.001 (Guo et al., 2025c).

articles.title: Network-based subbasin-scale mapping of streamflow alteration in Ontario, Canada
articles.titleEn: Network-based subbasin-scale mapping of streamflow alteration in Ontario, Canada
articles.abstract: Dams, reservoirs, waterpower facilities, and other water-control structures can modify streamflow and propagate their influence downstream through connected river networks, complicating hydrologic modelling and aquatic ecosystem assessment. Large-domain assessments often rely on binary agency classifications at hydrometric gauges (e.g., “natural” and “regulated”) or on storage- and discharge-based metrics that are difficult to apply consistently where operational data are incomplete. We introduce the Streamflow Alteration Index (SAI), a parsimonious, network-based screening metric that estimates the percentage of upstream drainage area whose routed flow passes through mapped alteration signal sources. Under a first-order drainage-area scaling approximation, SAI provides a proxy for the fraction of streamflow potentially exposed to upstream alteration sources, rather than a measure of the exact magnitude of hydrologic alteration. The framework comprises two paired indices, SAI_I (0 %–100 %) and SAI_II (0 %–100 %), independently representing confirmed Level I and potential Level II sources; values are propagated downstream by drainage-area-weighted mixing and reset at new sources of the same level. We compiled 2528 infrastructure records, of which 2476 were retained after geospatial alignment and screening. Following source classification and consolidation of multiple records within the same subbasin, 643 unique subbasins were identified as Level I and/or Level II alteration signal locations. The resulting SAI v1.0 database provides province-wide subbasin and river-reach layers for screening potential instream alteration at gauged and ungauged locations. We evaluated SAI-derived natural, conditional, and altered classes against 148 Reference Hydrometric Basin Network (RHBN) gauges, 125 additional Water Survey of Canada (WSC) gauges labelled natural, and 215 WSC-regulated gauges. SAI classified 86 % of both natural reference groups as natural, with no RHBN gauge classified as altered. Among WSC-regulated gauges, 26 % were classified as altered, 40 % as conditional, and 34 % as natural, highlighting differences between binary agency labels and the SAI screening framework and identifying sites requiring follow-up assessment. SAI v1.0 therefore provides a practical, transparent, and reproducible screening baseline for large-domain hydrologic and ecological applications without requiring detailed operating rules and offers a scalable framework for broader network-based assessments of potential streamflow alteration. The SAI v1.0 dataset is available from Zenodo (Shen et al., 2026; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19547932).

articles.title: Ten years of measurements (2012-2022) of the atmospheric composition at Saclay/SIRTA observatory in the Ile de France region as part of ICOS and ACTRIS
articles.titleEn: Ten years of measurements (2012-2022) of the atmospheric composition at Saclay/SIRTA observatory in the Ile de France region as part of ICOS and ACTRIS
articles.abstract: Carbon dioxide (CO 2 )is the main contributor to global warming, and cities now account for more than two-thirds of emissions of this gas. Atmospheric observatories located on the outskirts of cities are therefore important facilities for measuring the impact on atmospheric composition of the emission reductions planned by cities. The Saclay observatory, part of the ICOS and ACTRIS research infrastructures and located 20 km southwest of Paris, has been monitoring greenhouse gases (CO 2 , methane – CH 4 ), reactive gases (Nitrogen oxides – NO x , Ozone – O 3 , Carbon monoxide – CO), and carbonaceous aerosols (eBC) since 2012 (https://doi.org/10.57932/5c399263-a317-41b7-8900-184b177c4216, Bouillon and Ramonet, 2025). This study presents 10 years of monitoring of these compounds, characterizing diurnal, seasonal cycles and decadal trends. In order to best characterize the impact of Parisian emissions, we defined two sets of data depending on whether the station is downwind of Paris or, conversely, in background conditions with westerly winds. This strategy allows us to characterize the urban offset in the Saclay measurement series. The results show a significant decrease in the urban offset of compounds mainly linked to traffic emissions: −35.6 %, −52.3 %, and −56.7 % for CO, NO x , and eBC lf (equivalent black carbon from liquid fuel). There was also a 15 % decrease in urban offset of CO 2 between the 2012–2017 and 2019–2022 periods, a figure consistent with the Airparif inventories' estimate of the decrease in emissions in Paris over the same period.

articles.title: Review article: rainfall-induced landslide early warning systems through the lens of the early warnings for all framework – advances, gaps, and perspectives
articles.titleEn: Review article: rainfall-induced landslide early warning systems through the lens of the early warnings for all framework – advances, gaps, and perspectives
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: This review is necessary to provide a comprehensive evaluation of rainfall-induced landslide early warning systems (LEWS) through the lens of the United Nations “Early Warnings for All” (EW4All) framework. This study integrates EW4All pillars, examines information sharing in academic publications and official websites/portals, and evaluates the global feasibility of implementing EW4All for LEWS. Of 45 rainfall-induced systems, 27 (26 LEWS and one forecasting-focused system) were found operational (benefiting 19 countries), meaning they were implemented and actively used for warning purposes when this paper was prepared. Some forecasting-focused systems were misleadingly described as early warning systems. Among Local, Regional and National systems, Local systems were often less scalable and more resource-intensive. Operational systems were mainly National, followed by Regional. Most operational systems relied on rainfall thresholds. Some included susceptibility maps; risk maps were largely absent. Real-time sensor data were used in some systems; however, high maintenance costs limited scalability. Reliability was further constrained by data scarcity, limited forecast verification, and suboptimal use of Artificial Intelligence. Community engagement was infrequently documented in the reviewed systems. Although EW4All is transformative, implementing effective LEWS across rainfall-induced landslide-prone areas worldwide by 2027 remains impractical without localised approaches, sufficient funding, community engagement, and enhanced institutional capacity.

articles.title: Unravelling information on impactful geo-hydrological hazard events with HazMiner, a multilingual text mining method developed through a global scale coverage application
articles.titleEn: Unravelling information on impactful geo-hydrological hazard events with HazMiner, a multilingual text mining method developed through a global scale coverage application
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: The incidence and impacts of geo-hydrological hazards such as floods, flash floods and landslides are changing globally due to anthropogenic environmental changes and increased exposure driven by population growth. Reliable datasets on geo-hydrological hazards are essential to deepen our understanding of these hazards and their impacts. However, existing geo-hydrological hazard datasets contain data gaps leading to biased interpretations, especially in low- and lower-middle-income countries where populations are commonly the most impacted. Text mining offers new opportunities in documenting geo-hydrological hazards by automatically extracting information from large text corpora. Despite its potential, current methodologies are not adapted to improve documentation in data-scarce contexts. We introduce HazMiner, a paragraph-based text mining method designed to document the location, timing and impact of geo-hydrological hazards through transformer-based natural language processing models across multiple languages and at various scales. Applied here globally on 6 366 905 news articles published from 2017 through 2024 in 58 languages, HazMiner extracted 15 313 flood, 6836 landslide and 2258 flash flood events with a known location and time information and, in some cases, impact data. Compared to existing hazard datasets, HazMiner significantly improved hazard documentation, reducing the data gaps in many regions, especially in low- and lower-middle-income countries. This new versatile multilingual method and its dataset advance the accessibility and use of text mined natural hazard data.

articles.title: Microclimate, Vegetation, and Soil Response to Micro‐Zonal Solar Photovoltaic Patterning in a Humid Sub‐Tropical Agrivoltaic Grazing System
articles.titleEn: Microclimate, Vegetation, and Soil Response to Micro‐Zonal Solar Photovoltaic Patterning in a Humid Sub‐Tropical Agrivoltaic Grazing System
articles.abstract: Agrivoltaic grazing systems, or the integration of solar photovoltaic (PV) energy generation with livestock grazing, are the most common form of multi‐use solar energy in the United States and much of the world. However, there is a substantial gap in our understanding of the ecological impacts of combining PV and grazing in these novel ecosystems. Addressing this gap, we present data from the first 2 years of a study characterizing the interacting effects of PV infrastructure with land management (sheep grazing and mowing) in the Southeastern US. We observed spatial and temporal solar radiation and precipitation patterning among micro‐zones unique to the humid‐subtropical climate region and found that the PV modules maintained higher soil moisture than in the absence of PV, across all micro‐zones, with more dramatic differences observed during drier periods. Despite the significant patterning of microclimate conditions, we found no significant difference in above‐ground primary productivity across any micro‐zones or between management treatments within the array. Three years after construction, we detected no significant difference in soil carbon stocks across micro‐zones.

articles.title: Manhattan Pluvial Flood Simulations Under Two Extreme Rainfall Scenarios Show Similar Severity Patterns but Contrasting Peak Timing Across Districts
articles.titleEn: Manhattan Pluvial Flood Simulations Under Two Extreme Rainfall Scenarios Show Similar Severity Patterns but Contrasting Peak Timing Across Districts
articles.abstract: Urban pluvial flooding is often summarized by peak depth, peak extent, or cumulative burden, but these metrics do not distinguish when flooding first becomes hazardous from when the hazardous area becomes largest. This study introduces an activation–occupancy framework to quantify these two times and applies it to building‐resolving shallow‐water simulations of Manhattan ( at m resolution) under an Ida‐derived hyetograph and New York City's 1‐hr design storm. Under the Ida‐derived rainfall at the 0.3‐m threshold, district activation peaks occur within a 35‐min span, whereas the times of maximum hazard extent are much more dispersed. Under the shorter design storm, peak timing compresses sharply. Rainfall is spatially uniform in both simulations, so the 35‐min activation spread reflects routing alone and provides a lower bound on the variability of activation timing; spatial rainfall heterogeneity lies outside the modeled scenarios. Across the two modeled rainfall scenarios, severe‐flooding geography remains broadly consistent: the same seven districts exceed the borough reference at 0.2, 0.3, and 0.4 m, with the strongest rank preservation for eventual extent and hazardous area–time burden. At 0.5 m, that set contracts to six because Lower East Side/Chinatown falls just below the borough reference in both scenarios. East Harlem remains the principal exception in design‐storm timing at the deeper thresholds. These diagnostics distinguish severity patterns relevant to adaptation from scenario‐specific timing information for warning and response.

articles.title: Shallow Cumulus Cloud Statistics in Real‐Case Large‐Eddy Simulations and Their Dependence on Soil Moisture
articles.titleEn: Shallow Cumulus Cloud Statistics in Real‐Case Large‐Eddy Simulations and Their Dependence on Soil Moisture
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: The ability of weather and climate models to reproduce the statistical properties of shallow cumulus clouds (SCCs) is critical for representing boundary‐layer transport, cloud cover, and cloud‐radiative effects. This study investigates statistical properties of SCC ensembles using the Icosahedral Nonhydrostatic model in large‐eddy simulation mode for three cases during the Field Experiment on Submesoscale Spatio‐Temporal Variability in Lindenberg campaign. Feature‐based tracking is applied to identify cloud objects and track their evolution. Each cloud is classified as active or passive according to its in‐cloud buoyancy excess. The cloud‐base mass flux distribution of each class is robustly captured by a Weibull distribution. Active clouds exhibit shape parameters , consistent with convective memory related to their life‐cycle, while passive clouds approach , indicating stochastic, short‐lived nature. The bulk cloud‐base mass flux , representing the convective transport of the SCC population, scales linearly with surface heat input per unit cloud moist‐static‐energy excess, weighted by thermodynamic efficiency of the surface‐driven moist heat cycle. This scaling emerges primarily across the soil‐moisture perturbations and holds from moderately moisture‐limited to energy‐limited regimes, but linearity breaks down under very dry conditions, where a suppressed evaporative fraction and the resulting sub‐cloud moisture deficit prevent further increases in . Soil moisture strongly controls cloud number, updraft strength, cloud size, and the mass‐flux distribution, whereas responds to both soil‐moisture perturbations and day‐to‐day large‐scale conditions, highlighting land‐atmosphere coupling as a key regulator of shallow convective variability over land.

articles.title: Atmospheric stabilization of the East Antarctic ice sheet under warming
articles.titleEn: Atmospheric stabilization of the East Antarctic ice sheet under warming
articles.abstract: Most coupled Earth system models do not include fully interactive ice sheets, introducing uncertainty in future projections of polar climate and global sea level. To this end, we conduct 100,000-year-long simulations for different CO 2 conditions using the community Earth system model coupled to the bihemispheric Penn State University ice sheet–ice shelf model. Whereas global warming exceeding 2 °C above pre-industrial conditions and related subsurface ocean warming lead to the millennial-scale disintegration of the West Antarctic ice sheet, the East Antarctic ice sheet shows a much greater resilience, even at 10 °C or more of warming. The simulations reveal that a moister and cloudier atmosphere over Antarctica, with southward-shifted westerlies, increases snow accumulation and reduces shortwave radiation. For Greenland, a 6 °C threshold above pre-industrial levels is identified. Capturing the balance of ocean- and atmosphere-driven ablation and accumulation processes in coupled climate–ice-sheet models will improve projections of long-term sea-level rise.
